EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 131 
September 11, 1913. 
Mr. James D. Scott may be reinstated in the Railway Mail Service, without regard to the length of time he has been out of the service. The Postmaster General reports that he was appointed a railway mail clerk on October 17, 1900, at $800 per annum, and promoted through the successive grades until he received a salary of $1,100 per annum; that he resigned voluntarily, April 17,1911; that his record as a clerk is good, and his reinstatement would be to the benefit of the service. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending that an Executive order be issued in this case. 
September 17, 1913. 
Miss Emily W. Matter, of the District of Columbia, now temporarily employed in 
the same position through certification by the Civil Service Commission, may be appointed permanently to the position of clerk at $720 per annum in the Coast and 
Geodetic Survey. : The department in recommending this action stated that Miss Matter had demon- strated her fitness during temporary appointment, that the department had been 
unable to make selection from six certifications because of declinations and of the fact that many of the eligibles were found unsuitable. 
September 17, 1913. 
Mrs. Annie S. Renick, of the District of Columbia, may be appointed to the position of clerk at $1,000 per annum in the Department of State, without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. 
September 18, 1913. 
Mr. William B. Green may be reinstated as a compositor in the Weather Bureau without reference to the time limit imposed by the civil-service rules. 
Mr. Green’s services as a compositor were terminated on December 31, 1910, after more than 20 years’ service. The reason given at the time was that a reduction of the force was necessary because of the transfer of certain work from the Weather Bureau to the Government Printing Office. The Secretary of Agriculture with the concur- rence of the Civil Service Commission recommends the reinstatement because there is reason to believe that Mr. Green was unfairly dealt with because of certain testimony he had given in a case which resulted in the reprimand of the Chief of the Weather Bureau. 
September 18, 1913. 
Mr. David A. Robbins, formerly a letter carrier at Boston, Mass., may be reinstated as a letter carrier in the Postal Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service. 
Mr. Robbins was appointed a substitute letter carrier February 15, 1900; appointed a carrier December 30, 1902, at $600; promoted to $800 December 30, 1903; resigned April 28, 1904; reinstated as senior substitute carrier November 15, 1904; promoted to carrier at $800 November 22, 1904; promoted to $1,000 November 22, 1905; pro- moted to $1,100 July 1, 1907; promoted to $1,200 July 1, 1908; reduced to $1,100 August 1, 1910; resigned October 31, 1910, for personal reasons. He made application for reinstatement in a letter dated May 17, 1911, and in reply was informed of the con- ditions of the reinstatement rule and that his application must be renewed through the postmaster in order to receive consideration. On October 15, 1912, he made a second request for reinstatement. The Postmaster General states that from the facts presented, it would seem that an Executive order reinstating Mr. Robbins in the service would be warranted. The Civil Service Commission does not recommend this order. 
October 1, 1913. 
Mrs. Mary D. Hanna may be appointed to a clerkship in the classified service subject to such tests of fitness as the Civil Service Commission may require. Mrs. Hanna is the widow of Capt. Guy B. G. Hanna, Coast Artillery, who met his death while in the line of duty, by the premature explosion of a service charge during night target practice. In view of the tragic circumstances of the case and the fact that it 18 now necessary for Mrs. Hanna to earn her own livelihood the Secretary of War recommended the issuance of an Executive order waiving the requirement of exami- nation under the civil-service rules to permit her appointment. The Civil Service Commission recommended that the appointment be permitted, subject to appropriate tests of fitness,

EXECUTIVE ORDERS. 133 
October 22, 1913. 
Mrs. Mary R. Geddings may be appointed to a position in the classified service with 
out reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. Mrs. Geddings is the widow of Surg. Henry D. Geddings, of the Public Health Serv- ice, who was a commissioned medical officer in that service for about 25 years, and who rendered distinguished service in matters relating to sanitation and public health. 
He also rendered valuable service in several epidemics of yellow fever at a time when few medical men were immune to that disease and its cause was but little known. The Secretary of the Treasury states that it would be a fitting testimonial to the serv- ices of Surg. Geddings to waive the civil-service rules to permit the appointment of Mrs. Geddings in the classified service. The Civil Service Commission does not 
recommend that an Executive order be issued in this case. 
October 23, 1913. 
Mr. Henry J. Cokayne may be reinstated as a mail carrier in the Postal Service without regard to the length of his separation from the service. This order is issued for the reason that Mr. Cokayne’s dismissal does not appear to have been warranted by the facts. His reinstatement is recommended by the post- office inspector who made an investigation of the case, and by the First Assistant Postmaster General. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending 
that an Executive order be issued authorizing the reinstatement of Mr. Cokayne. 
October 24, 1913. 
Mr. Solon J. Boughton may be reinstated as assistant examiner in the Patent Office, Department of the Interior, without reference to the period of his separation from the service. Mr. Boughton served as an assistant patent examiner from December 1, 1907, to August 9, 1911. He resigned for the purpose of taking up his residence in Colorado when it was found that he had contracted tuberculosis. A cure was effected within a 
short time and during his period of eligibility he communicated with the Patent Office relative to reinstatement but was ad vised to remain in Colorado and was promised that a recommendation would be made for his reinstatement when he desired to resume his duties. The Secretary of the Interior recommends the reinstatement on account of Mr. Boughton’s experience and the fact that he served with great ability. The Civil 
Service Commission concurs in recommending this Executive order. 
October 29, 1913. 
Mr. John H. Jenkins

October 22, 1913.

out reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. Mrs. Geddings is the widow of Surg. Henry D. October 24, 1913. 
Mr. Solon J. Boughton may be reinstated as assistant examiner in the Patent Office, Department of the Interior, without reference to the period of his separation from the service. 122 THIRTY-FIRST REPORT U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION. 
December 5, 1913. 
Mr. Herbert L. Solyom may be reinstated as an assistant examiner in the Patent Office, the year limit upon eligibility in his case being waived. Mr. Solyom served four and one-half years as an assistant examiner in the Patent Office, resigning on August 9, 1907, to accept the position of chief forecaster in the meteorological office of the Argentine Republic. While employed as assistant exam- iner in the Patent Office he displayed unusual ability and scientific attainments, his work being excellent as to quality and quantity. A man of Mr. Solyom’s experience is more valuable than a new appointee would be within three or four years. In view of the technical character of the position of assistant examiner and the evident qualifications of Mr. Solyom for the position, the Civil Service Commission joins with the Secretary of the Interior in recommending an Executive order waiving the year limit, to permit his reinstatement. 
December 10, 1913. 
Mr. George P. Herndon may be appointed to a clerkship in the Bureau of the Census, Department of Commerce, at $1,000 per annum, without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. Mr. Herndon was appointed a clerk at $900 per annum in the Bureau of the Census on June 1, 1900; promoted to $1,000 September 1, 1900; and to $1,200 November 15, 1901. His services were discontinued June 30, 1902. This order is issued in view of the satisfactory service rendered by Mr. Herndon in the Twelfth Census and the statement of the Director of the Census that he would be glad to recommend the reinstatement of Mr. Herndon, which the Secretary of Com- merce approves. 
December 18, 1913. 
Mr. Alfred Freeman, of New Jersey, may be appointed clerk in the postal service without reference to the requirement of examination under the civil-service rules. This order is issued at the suggestion of the Postmaster General on account of the great increase in the handling of packages due to the introduction of the parcel post. Mr. Freeman has had more than 12 years’ experience supervising the delivery of small packages and the handling of a large force of men. 
December 22, 1913. 
Mr. Albert K. Brown, now employed as a classified laborer in the Bureau of Fish and Fisheries, may be promoted to the position of clerk at $1,200 per annum without examination under the civil-service rules. Mr. Brown has for years performed without promotion work of a character that would justify much larger pay. This action is taken on account of Mr. Brown’s experience and his admitted intelligence, skill, and exceptional ability for the position for which his promotion is proposed. His promotion is recommended by the Secretary of Commerce, which is concurred in by Mr. Brown’s superiors in the Bureau of Fish and Fisheries. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending 
that an Executive order be issued in this case. 
December 22, 1913. 
Mrs. Mary Hill Dunn may be appointed as a clerk in the Navy Department without compliance with the civil-service rules. Mrs. Dunn is the wife of Mr. Charles A. Dunn, who was employed in the Secretary’s office of the Navy Department for a period of over 23 years, he having resigned March 15, 1909, as clerk at $1,800 per annum, on account of the fact that he was afflicted with tuberculosis. For the greater portion of the period since that date he has been confined at the naval hospital, Las Animas, Colo., and his wife and two small children are without means of support. While employed in the Navy Department Mr. Dunn rendered efficient service, and was considered one of the most valuable clerks in the office. Mrs. Dunn has had considerable experience in office work outside the Gov￾ernment service, and was recently temporarily employed in the Census Office and the Pension Office. The Secretary of the Navy is satisfied that she is well qualified to perform the duties of a clerkship, and recommends that an Executive os be issued authorizing her appointment. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in the recommendation. 
December 22, 1913. 
Mr. Herbert L. Halter may be appointed a rural carrier at Hershey, Nebr., without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Halter was a clerk in the Navy Department from June 19. 1909, to September 27, 1911. His separation was due to his having contracted tuberculosis, and he has

since received treatment at the naval hospital at Las Animas, Colo. The disease has been arrested, but it is necessary that he remain in a climate which is similar. His appointment as rural carrier was requested by the Secretary of the Navy and is con￾curred in by the Postmaster General and the Civil Service Commission. 
December 22, 1913. 
Miss Anita H. Stephens, formerly an employee in the Philippine civil service, may be appointed to the position of clerk (first grade) in the Department of Commerce, without further examination under the civil-service rules. Miss Stephens was formerly employed in the Library of Congress and was trans- ferred to the position of assistant librarian in the bureau of science at Manila, at an annual compensation of $1,400, the Civil Seivice Commission having certified that she had submitted evidence of her training and experience from which it appeared that she had the requisite qualifications to render her eligible for appointment. In view of the excellent service of Miss Stephens in the Philippines and the fact that the condition of her health made it necessary for her to leave the islands two months before the expiration of the three-year period of service which would have rendered her eligible for transfer this order is issued. The transfer and appointment of Miss Stephens is recommended by the Assistant Secretary of War and the Chief of the Bureau of Insular Affairs, and is concurred in by the Secretary of Commerce. The Civil Service Commission does not concur in recommending that an order be issued in this case. 
January 19, 1914. 
Miss Edith P. Johnson may be continued as chief operator of a billing machine in the office of the appraiser of merchandise at the port of New York without reference to the civil-service rules. Miss Johnson has served in this position since November 16, 1911, and because of her fidelity and industry and certain unusual features of the case, the Civil Service Commission joins with the Treasury Department in recommending this order. 
January 24, 1914. 
Mr. Francis H. Duehay may be appointed superintendent of prisons, Department of Justice, without reference to the civil service rules. This order is issued upon the recommendation of the Attorney General, who believes that Mr. Duehay is especially qualified for the position, which requires a peculiar order of talent. The Civil Service Commission concurs in the recommendation.
